extracted.intended_audience: USPTO management, patent examiners, patent applicants, and stakeholders concerned with RCE backlog and patent quality assurance
extracted.subtask_description: Audit findings, standards, and recommendations regarding USPTO practices for handling Requests for Continued Examination (RCEs), introduction of new prior art in final rejections, production credit/docket policies, and quality assurance. Focused on managing RCE pendency, examiner incentives, and initiatives to reduce RCEs.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP 706.07(a) rule on new prior art in final rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Under current USPTO policy, as set forth in the Manual of Patent Examining Procedure (MPEP) 706.07(a), patent examiners are allowed to issue final rejections after an applicant responds to examiner comments and/or amends an application. However, examiners may only provide new prior art in a final rejection if an amendment necessitated citation of the new ground or if the new ground was cited in an information disclosure statement filed during the period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO management noted examiners should not include references to new prior art to reject claims that were not substantively amended by the applicant. The OIG random sample of 50 final rejections found examiners introduced new prior art but only in response to amended claims; no instances were found where new prior art was applied to unamended claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: PTO-892 as a risk indicator for new prior art introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner prepares form PTO-892, 'Notice of References Cited,' the examiner is listing existing or new references he or she deems pertinent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preparing PTO-892 with the final rejection is a strong indicator that the examiner is likely including new prior art in the final rejection. OPQA does not specifically target PTO-892 cases in its QA sampling, which may reduce the likelihood of catching inappropriate new prior art introductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: OPQA statistical-sample QA approach and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: OPQA reviews a statistical sample from all final rejections and approved patent applications to test whether examiners applied the proper prior art. OPQA reviews several thousand applications each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While OPQA's approach produces a statistically robust estimate of error rates (USPTO found 1.8% of final rejections had examiner error related to inappropriate introduction of new prior art), it does not target subpopulations most at risk (e.g., PTO-892 flagged actions), and OPQA cannot always know if an application it reviewed will later have an RCE because RCEs may be filed after OPQA performs checks. The OIG suggests OPQA consider stratified samples targeting risk areas to better detect specific instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production credit alignment influences examiner priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO gives production credit to examiners for specific actions; production credit values and docketing affect which tasks examiners prioritize.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy changes that increased credit for reviewing new applications relative to RCEs (and removed strict time requirements for RCEs) incentivized examiners to focus on new applications, contributing to RCE backlog growth. Adjusting credits without corresponding target changes can reduce overall productivity and devalue certain work products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific production credit/docketing policy changes (FY2010–FY2014)
rubrics_metrics.description: Before FY2010 changes, examiners received same production credit for reviewing new applications and RCEs; after changes, examiners received more credit for new applications than for RCEs. Docket rules requiring examiners to respond to an RCE within 2 months were lifted; some examiners were required to review as few as 13 RCEs each year. April 2013 'fire sale' and FY2014 agreement temporarily altered credits (examples: FY2013 Q1–2 RCE credit 1.75 vs new application credit 2.0; FY2014 arrangements provided inflated credits for certain RCE reviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete credit values and docketing rule changes materially shifted examiner behavior, increased RCE pendency and backlog, and in some periods reduced total office actions by examiners. Any future changes should consider impacts on productivity, inventory mix, and statutory timing requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory 4-month RCE response requirement (35 U.S.C. §154(b)(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a 4-month response time required by law for RCEs as established by 35 U.S.C. §154(b)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If USPTO fails to respond within this time period, the patent term is extended (subject to limitations). The report documents average applicant wait for preliminary RCE decisions increasing from 48 days to almost 210 days between January 2008 and January 2013, highlighting risk of patent term adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for strategic RCE inventory goals and trigger thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO had not established strategic goals outlining what a manageable RCE inventory should consist of relative to the size of its examiner corps or thresholds for backlog or pendency fluctuations that would trigger management action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without these thresholds or automatic triggers, management reacted slowly to RCE growth. Establishing clear, quantitative thresholds would enable timelier, situation-specific responses and inform negotiations with the union and IT/system changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: research variance in after-final amendment approval and filings
rubrics_metrics.description: Research the reasons for the variance in after-final amendment approval rates and the precipitous decline in after-final amendment filings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding why after-final amendments are less common or less successful could identify process or training changes to reduce RCE filings and improve compact prosecution outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: assess examiner-grade differences in RCE rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess why applications handled by lower- and higher-grade examiners have different RCE filing rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis by examiner grade could reveal training, workload, or incentive mismatches that influence RCE filing behavior and may inform targeted interventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: assess art-unit variance and identify best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the reasons for variance among art units, identify best practices that promote efficiency, and then develop strategies to minimize patent term adjustment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Art-unit-level differences may point to transferable practices; formalizing and disseminating best practices could reduce RCEs and pendency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: determine value of stratified QA sampling targeting risk areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether a stratified sample of patent applications targeting risk areas, such as applications with new prior art applied in a final rejection, would enhance quality assurance tests and the overall determination of patent examiner quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeting high-risk strata (e.g., PTO-892 flagged cases) could increase detection of inappropriate practices even if overall error rates remain low in broad statistical samples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: establish a risk management plan for RCE handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish a risk management plan that ensures timely, situation-specific analysis and solutions are documented and implemented to minimize patent-term adjustments when rebalancing is needed to meet statutory requirements and public expectations for prompt processing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A documented risk management approach should include thresholds, actions, roles, and timelines so that rebalancing (e.g., via credit/docket changes) does not cause unintended patent-term extensions or quality degradation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation: increase participation in compact prosecution initiatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop ways to increase participation in the compact prosecution initiatives, especially AFCP 2.0, and continue efforts to engage all stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low applicant participation in Quick Path Information Disclosure Statement (QPIDS), AFCP 2.0, and First Action Interview Pilot (FAIP) dampens their potential to reduce RCEs; targeted outreach and program design changes could increase opt-in rates and reduce RCE likelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: QPIDS program participation and purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: QPIDS is a pilot program to address a niche issue. QPIDS allows applicants to disclose prior art that may be relevant to the patent application to avoid an additional RCE review. To participate in QPIDS, applicants must pay a fee and file several forms, including a transmittal form that designates the request as a QPIDS submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because QPIDS participants would otherwise need to go through the RCE review process if not participating, OPQA could not directly compare QPIDS effects in the same way as other pilots. Participation levels were low (2,480 tracked May 2012–Nov 2013).

rubrics_metrics.name: AFCP 2.0 program participation requirements and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: AFCP 2.0 is a pilot program focused on obtaining agreement through after-final amendments. To opt into AFCP 2.0, applicants must file a request for consideration under the pilot and amend at least one independent claim that does not broaden the scope of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AFCP 2.0 participation substantially lowered the probability an applicant would file an RCE—holding other variables constant, participation lowers likelihood by almost 20 percentage points. Supervisors noted benefits (allows interviews to resolve issues) and limitations (applicants may not sufficiently narrow claims; examiners may lack time to review after-final amendments). Participation was tracked at 16,598 (May–Nov 2013) but underutilized.

rubrics_metrics.name: FAIP program participation requirements and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: First Action Interview Pilot (FAIP) allows the applicant and examiner to meet before the first action. To participate, an applicant must file a request at least one day before the first office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participation lowered likelihood of RCE filing by about 7 percentage points. Participation tracked at 4,169 (Oct 2005–Nov 2013). FAIP and AFCP 2.0 both reduce RCE likelihood but have low overall opt-in rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: After-final amendment limitations and prosecution rights
rubrics_metrics.description: After-final amendments are amendments filed by applicants after the examiner has issued a final rejection. Examiners may choose to approve applications following after-final amendments; however, they are not required to provide new determinations in response to after-final amendments if the amendment is not entered by the examiner. Once a final rejection that is not premature has been entered in an application, there is no right to unrestricted further prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural constraint limits applicants' ability to rely on after-final amendments to avoid RCEs, and explains part of the dynamics leading applicants to file RCEs instead of or after after-final amendments.
